items.title: Europe's Ariane 64 rocket to make maiden launch Thursday

featured_image.name: ESA - Ariane 6 stands tall on its launch pad

items.description:
Europe's most powerful rocket is poised to make history. On Thursday, the Ariane 64 rocket will lift off from the European spaceport in Kourou, French Guiana, marking the first flight of the four-booster configuration and carrying 32 satellites for Amazon Leo's broadband internet constellation.

The mission, designated VA267 by Arianespace, will open a launch window at 4:45 p.m. UTC, with the window closing at 5:13 p.m. UTC. The flight represents the first in a series of 18 missions contracted by Amazon to deploy its low Earth orbit satellite network, designed to compete with SpaceX's Starlink service.[1][2][3][4][5]

items.title: Study finds half of world's coral reefs bleached in 2014-17

featured_image.name: Coral reefs suffer fourth global bleaching event, NOAA says ...

items.description:
More than half of the world's coral reefs were bleached during a prolonged marine heatwave from 2014 to 2017, according to a study published Tuesday in the journal Nature Communications. The research represents the first comprehensive global analysis of what scientists have named the Third Global Bleaching Event, confirming it as the most severe coral die-off ever recorded.

The international team of researchers estimated that 51 percent of the world's reef areas suffered moderate or greater bleaching during the three-year period, with 15 percent experiencing substantial mortality. The findings paint a grim picture that scientists warn is already being surpassed by an ongoing fourth global bleaching event.

items.title: Study: Climate change could halve global grazing land by 2100

featured_image.name: Study sheds lighton global risk ofheat stress to cattle

items.description:
Up to half of the world's grasslands suitable for cattle, sheep, and goat farming could become unviable by the end of the century due to rising global temperatures, according to a major new study that warns of severe consequences for more than 100 million pastoralists and up to 1.6 billion livestock worldwide.

The research, published in the journal PNAS on February 9, was led by scientists at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany. It identifies a "safe climatic space" for grazing systems that cover roughly one-third of Earth's land surface and represent the world's largest food production system.[1][2][3]

items.title: Yen extends gains as Takaichi's landslide win reshapes Japan markets

featured_image.name: Sanae Takaichi set to become Japan's first female prime minister

items.description:
The Japanese yen extended gains against the US dollar on Tuesday as markets digested Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's historic election victory, while the greenback remained under pressure ahead of key American economic releases this week.

The USD/JPY pair fell to around 155.50 on Tuesday morning, continuing a slide that began after the ruling Liberal Democratic Party secured a supermajority in Sunday's snap election. The yen's appreciation marked a reversal of the pre-election trend that had pushed the currency toward the closely watched 160 level against the dollar.[1][2]

items.title: Satellite images show Iran burying nuclear site entrances

featured_image.name: Satellite images show all entrances to Iran's Isfahan ...

items.description:
Satellite imagery captured this week shows that Iran has completely buried all three tunnel entrances at its Isfahan nuclear complex with soil, in a move that analysts say mirrors defensive preparations taken before American strikes devastated the facility last year.

The Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security (ISIS) published high-resolution images taken Sunday showing the middle and southern tunnel entrances at the site are now "unrecognizable and fully covered in soil," while the northernmost entrance—which had already been fitted with additional defensive measures—has also been backfilled. No vehicle or personnel activity is visible around the entrances, according to the institute.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Satellite data reveals faster methane breakdown in stratosphere

featured_image.name: Private satellites pinpoint methane emissions from oil, gas and coal facilities worldwide

items.description:
University of Washington researchers have produced the first satellite-based estimate of methane destruction in the stratosphere, finding that the powerful greenhouse gas breaks down at a higher rate than climate models previously predicted. The study, published Sunday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, offers new clarity on how methane accumulates in Earth's atmosphere—a long-standing puzzle for climate scientists.[1][2]

The finding addresses a persistent gap between two methods of calculating global methane levels that have historically produced conflicting results. By replacing model-based estimates with satellite observations, the researchers brought the two approaches into close agreement for the first time.[3][2]

items.title: January 2026 ranks fifth-warmest on record despite polar extremes

featured_image.name: Coldest January in 16 years - The Berliner

items.description:
Europe recorded its coldest January since 2010 as polar vortex disruptions sent Arctic air flooding across the continent, while the Southern Hemisphere simultaneously endured deadly heatwaves and wildfires, according to new data from the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service released Tuesday.

Despite the sharp regional contrasts, global temperatures remained near record levels. January 2026 was the fifth-warmest January on record, with a global average surface temperature of 12.95 degrees Celsius—just 0.28 degrees Celsius cooler than January 2025, the warmest January ever recorded.[1][2][3]

items.title: Honda's quarterly operating profit drops 61% on tariffs, EV woes

featured_image.name: Honda Motor reports 76% plunge in operating profit in huge earnings miss

items.description:
Honda Motor reported a 42 percent drop in nine-month net profit on Tuesday, as the Japanese automaker continued to struggle under the weight of U.S. import tariffs, weakening electric vehicle demand, and ongoing chip supply disruptions.

Net profit for the nine months ended December fell to 465.44 billion yen ($2.99 billion), down from 805.26 billion yen in the same period a year earlier, according to the company's earnings report. Nine-month revenue declined 2.2 percent to 15.976 trillion yen.[1][2]

items.title: Oil eases as traders assess supply risks from US-Iran tensions

featured_image.name: Oil Can Hit $91 a Barrel in Late 2026 on Iran Disruption

items.description:
Oil prices eased slightly on Tuesday as traders weighed the potential for supply disruptions after the United States issued fresh guidance for commercial vessels navigating the Strait of Hormuz, maintaining attention on simmering tensions between Washington and Tehran over Iran's nuclear program.

Brent crude futures and West Texas Intermediate both fell by roughly 0.4% in early trading, according to Reuters. The modest pullback followed a more than 1% rise on Monday when the U.S. Department of Transportation's Maritime Administration released the new shipping advisory.[1][2]

items.title: DP World boss in Dubai exchanged personal and business emails with Jeffrey Epstein for years

featured_image.name: H.E Sultan Ahmed Bin Sulayem, Group Chairman and CEO, DP World

items.description:
Sultan Ahmed bin Sulayem, the chairman and chief executive of global logistics giant DP World, maintained a close correspondence with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein for more than a decade after Epstein's 2008 conviction, according to documents released by the U.S. Department of Justice. The emails show the Dubai executive discussing sexual experiences with women and, in some cases, sharing information about prostitution services while abroad.

The disclosures emerge from more than 3 million pages of Epstein-related files released by the Justice Department on January 30 under the Epstein Files Transparency Act. Bin Sulayem stands out among the prominent figures named in the documents for the longevity of his exchanges with the disgraced financier, which continued until less than a year before Epstein's death in a New York jail cell in 2019.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Sydney researchers use liquid gallium to produce hydrogen from seawater

featured_image.name: Scientists use sunlight and liquid metal to produce clean ...

items.description:
Researchers at the University of Sydney have developed a method to produce clean hydrogen from both seawater and freshwater using liquid gallium powered by sunlight, offering a circular approach that could help advance Australia's green hydrogen ambitions.

The process, detailed in a paper published in Nature Communications in January, uses photothermal oxidation to heat liquid gallium droplets under light exposure, triggering a reaction with water that produces hydrogen and gallium oxyhydroxide. The gallium oxyhydroxide can then be electrochemically reduced back into gallium for reuse, creating what the researchers call a "circular" hydrogen production method.[1][2][3]

items.title: Air Canada halts Cuba flights as fuel crisis deepens

featured_image.name: Air Canada suspends flights to Cuba because of aviation fuel shortage

items.description:
Cuba enacted drastic emergency measures on Monday as the island nation grapples with a rapidly worsening energy crisis exacerbated by U.S. pressure to cut off its oil supply. The government has mandated a four-day workweek for state-owned companies, reduced school hours, suspended university classes, and slashed public transportation services while restricting fuel sales.[1][2][3][4]

The emergency protocols took effect as Havana's streets fell notably silent, with the communist government scrambling to preserve rapidly depleting fuel reserves. Air Canada announced Monday it is suspending all flights to Cuba after Cuban authorities warned that aviation fuel would no longer be available at the island's airports beginning Tuesday, February 10.[5][6][4]

items.title: Israel warns US it may strike Iran alone over missile threat

featured_image.name: Netanyahu to meet Trump in Washington Wednesday to discuss ...

items.description:
Israeli defense officials have told their American counterparts that Jerusalem is prepared to launch unilateral military strikes against Iran's ballistic missile infrastructure if Tehran crosses what Israel considers a critical security threshold, according to multiple reports citing security sources.

"We told the Americans we will strike alone if Iran crosses the red line we set on ballistic missiles," a senior Israeli source told The Jerusalem Post, adding that Israel has not yet reached that threshold but is continuously monitoring developments inside Iran. The officials described Iran's expanding missile capabilities as an existential threat and outlined operational plans to dismantle key manufacturing sites and production facilities.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Alphabet raises $20B in bond sale amid record AI-driven demand

featured_image.name: 2+ Hundred Alphabet Inc Headquarters Royalty-Free Images ...

items.description:
Alphabet, the parent company of Google, sold $20 billion in bonds on Monday in a deal that attracted more than $100 billion in investor orders, underscoring the enormous appetite for debt tied to the artificial intelligence boom.[1][2]

The seven-part offering of senior unsecured notes exceeded the company's initial expectations of $15 billion, with demand described by Bloomberg as among the strongest ever for a corporate bond offering. Alphabet is also planning an additional sterling bond sale that may include a rare 100-year "century bond," which would mark the first such long-dated debt issued by a technology company since the dot-com era.[3][4][5][1]

items.title: Cuba halts airline refueling for a month amid energy crisis

featured_image.name: Airlines will no longer be able to refuel on Cuba as U.S. blockade ...

items.description:
Cuba has notified international carriers that aviation fuel will be unavailable across the island's airports for an entire month, forcing major airlines to suspend or reroute flights as the nation's energy crisis reaches a critical stage.

The Cuban government issued an official Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) on Sunday evening warning that Jet A-1 fuel will not be available from February 10 through March 11 at all nine international airports, including Havana's José Martí International Airport, Varadero, Santa Clara, Holguín, Santiago de Cuba, and Cayo Coco. The measure is expected to disrupt more than 400 scheduled weekly flights.[1][2][3][4][5]

items.title: Bennu asteroid samples challenge theory on how life's building blocks formed

featured_image.name: Life's ingredients have been found in samples from asteroid ...

items.description:
Amino acids, the molecular building blocks essential for life, may have formed in icy, radiation-rich conditions at the edge of the early solar system rather than in warm water, according to new research published today in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The findings, based on analysis of samples from asteroid Bennu returned to Earth by NASA's OSIRIS-REx mission in 2023, challenge decades of assumptions about how life's basic ingredients first arose.

"Our results flip the script on how we have typically thought amino acids formed in asteroids," said Allison Baczynski, assistant research professor of geosciences at Penn State and co-lead author of the study. "It now looks like there are many conditions where these building blocks of life can form, not just when there's warm liquid water."[1][2]

items.title: Mexico suspends oil shipments to Cuba to avoid US tariffs

featured_image.name: Mexico to send oil to Cuba despite Trump pressure - Bloomberg

items.description:
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum confirmed on Monday that Mexico has suspended oil shipments to Cuba to avoid tariffs threatened by the Trump administration, calling the US sanctions "very unfair" as she warned that the measures would "strangle" the crisis-stricken island nation.

"This sanction being imposed on countries that sell oil to Cuba is very unfair... sanctions that harm the people are not right," Sheinbaum told reporters at her daily press briefing. "You cannot strangle a people like this—it's very unfair, very unfair."[1]

items.title: US, Bangladesh sign trade deal cutting tariffs to 19%

featured_image.name: US strikes new deal with Bangladesh to trim tariff rate on ...

items.description: The United States and Bangladesh have signed a trade agreement reducing US tariffs on Bangladeshi goods to 19 percent and establishing a mechanism for duty-free treatment of certain apparel products made with American materials. The deal, finalized Monday, comes just days before Bangladesh holds its first general election since the ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in 2024.

items.title: Trump to visit China in April for Xi summit

featured_image.name: Trump, Xi discuss Taiwan and soybeans in call aimed at easing China, US relations

items.description:
U.S. President Donald Trump will travel to Beijing during the first week of April for a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, according to a Politico report citing three people familiar with the plans. The trip would mark the first visit by a sitting American president to China since Trump's own 2017 state visit during his first term.[1][2]

The visit comes as the world's two largest economies seek to stabilize relations following months of trade tensions, including an $11 billion U.S. arms deal with Taiwan and Chinese military exercises surrounding the island. Trump has described the upcoming trip as a "business trip" aimed at securing further trade wins.[3][2]

items.title: Eight Muslim nations condemn Israel's West Bank annexation moves

featured_image.name: Israel approves biggest expansion of West Bank settlements ...

items.description:
Eight predominantly Muslim countries issued a joint statement on Monday condemning Israel's newly approved measures in the occupied West Bank, calling them illegal annexation attempts that violate international law and threaten regional stability.

The foreign ministers of Turkey, Egypt, Jordan, Indonesia, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates denounced Israel's Sunday decision as an effort to impose "unlawful Israeli sovereignty, entrenching settlement activity, and enforcing a new legal and administrative reality in the occupied West Bank, thereby accelerating attempts at its illegal annexation and the displacement of the Palestinian people."[1][2]

The joint statement, posted on the Turkish Foreign Ministry's website, emphasized that "Israel has no sovereignty over the occupied Palestinian territory" and warned that such actions "fuel violence and conflict in the region."[1]
